final_message:
All three versions are done and pass every sample.

**Algorithm.** Each step is the specified semi-implicit Euler update. The wrap spring force `f[N-1]` is computed first. It is also `f[-1]` for mass 0. That makes the ring update straightforward without a separate rotated array. Final energies, position sum, and first index of maximum `|v|` are computed as specified. `N=1` and `S=0` are handled explicitly.

**Speed choices**

- [Rust version](/C:/Users/sandh/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder-full/springs/rust/src/main.rs): contiguous `Vec<f64>` arrays. Precomputes `dt/m[i]` once, replacing 60 million divisions with multiplications. On x86_64 it runtime-detects AVX2 and uses two 4-lane passes per step. Spring forces are stored shifted by one, so `f[i]` and `f[i-1]` are simple offset loads. A scalar fallback handles other CPUs and tails. The release profile in [the Cargo manifest](/C:/Users/sandh/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder-full/springs/rust/Cargo.toml) uses fat LTO and one codegen unit.
- [Plain Python version](/C:/Users/sandh/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder-full/springs/plain.py): lists of floats and one fused forward pass per step. It carries `f[i-1]` in a local variable. Writing `x[i]` in that pass cannot corrupt any spring force still needed. It precomputes `a=dt/m` and `b=1-a*c`, so the inner loop has no division. All hot values are locals.
- [NumPy version](/C:/Users/sandh/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder-full/springs/fast.py): contiguous `float64` arrays and reused buffers. About nine in-place ufunc calls run per step, with no per-step allocation and no `np.roll`. It uses the same precomputed `a` and `b` regrouping as the plain version.

The Python regrouping and Rust `dt/m` hoisting change only last-ulp rounding. On a generated `N=4000, S=15000` input, their outputs agreed with the exact formula to about `1e-13` relative. This is well within the `1e-9` tolerance.

**Testing.** All three versions pass all five samples: `s1a`, `s1b`, `s1c`, `s2`, and `s3`. Every `fastest` index matches exactly. The largest sample error was about `3.4e-13` relative. I also cross-checked the three versions against each other on random cases with `N` from 1 to 401, including `S=0`. All agreed.

**Indicative benchmark.** On a generated benchmark-size input, whole-process times were roughly 0.10-0.12 s for Rust, 0.65-0.79 s for NumPy, and 21 s for plain Python. The machine was busy with other work, so treat these as indicative only.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
